newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Kueste state metalworkers see sick pay pact.
newsitem.headline: German Kueste state metalworkers see sick pay pact.

text.p: Metal and engineering trade union officials in the north German region of Kueste said on Tuesday they hoped to have a wage agreement guaranteeing full sick pay for the some 190,000 workers in the sector there.

Their optimism follows the break-through deal signed last week in the state of Lower Saxony in which metal and engineering employers agreed not to implement a controversial new law cutting sick pay entitlements by 20 percent.
"I cannot imagine that Kueste will not be able to manage what Lower Saxony did as the mould-breaker," Frank Teichmueller, head of the IG Metall trade union in the region, told journalists on Tuesday.

Tecihmueller said however that early talks had ran into conflict on the issue of job protection measures. Employers were now questioning a previously-discussed scheme under which work councils could demand that companies reduce working hours before making redundancies, he said.
A spokesman for the employer negotiators had earlier said he nonetheless believed a wage pact would be agreed similar to the Lower Saxony deal.

IG Metall hailed last Thursday's agreement, which itself only applies to the some 90,000 workers in the region, as a break-through after protests that have involved hundreds of thousands of workers in the three-million-strong sector.

Under the Lower Saxony package, workers will receive a 1.5 percent rise in 1997 salaries and a 2.5 percent increase in 1998. In return for maintaining full sick pay, workers have agreed to lower Christmas bonuses.
Employers said that while they had to back down on plans to make sick pay cuts, the package meant that overall labour costs would rise by less than one percent next year.
Negotiations in other regions are also going ahead this week in the central state of Hesse and the large southern region of Bavaria.
No early agreement was however seen as likely in either region.

German engineering employers in part of the southern German region of Baden-Wuerttemberg had said on Monday they would thrash out their own wage agreement for the 300,000 workers there rather than adopt the accord reached in Lower Saxony.
